Special provisions Trade Disputes Act An Act relating to trade disputes Commencement date: 21 January 1962 Part I Preliminary Article 1 Short title This Act may be cited as the Trade Disputes Act.
Article 2 Interpretation In this Act— “intimidation” means, as reasonably understood by a person, an intention to cause injury to him or to any member of his family or to any person dependent on him, or violence or trespass to any person or property;
“injury” includes damage to a person's business, occupation, employment or other source of income, and includes any actionable wrong;
“lock-out” means the closing of a place of employment or the suspension of work, or the refusal by an employer to continue to employ any number of persons employed by him in consequence of a dispute, done with a view to compelling those persons, or to aiding another employer in compelling persons employed by him, to accept terms or conditions of or affecting employment;
“registered” means registered under the Trade Unions Act.
“strike” means the cessation of work by a body of persons employed acting in combination, or a concerted refusal or a refusal under a common understanding of any number of persons employed to continue to work for an employer in consequence of a dispute, done as a means of compelling their employer or any person or body of persons employed, or to aid other persons employed in compelling their employer or any person or body of persons employed, to accept or not to accept terms or conditions of or affecting employment;
“trade dispute” means any dispute between employers and workmen, or between workmen and workmen, which is connected with the employment or non-employment or the terms of employment or with the conditions of labour of any person;
“trade union” means any combination, whether temporary or permanent, the principal objects of which are under its constitution the regulating of the relations between workmen and employers, or between workmen and workmen, or between employers and employers, whether such combination would or would not, if this Act had not been enacted, have been deemed to have been an unlawful combination by reason of some one or more of its purposes being in restraint of trade;
“tribunal” means a tribunal appointed and constituted under section 19;
“workman” means any person who has entered into or works under a contract with an employer, whether the employer is or is not a body corporate, and whether the contract is express or implied, oral or written, and whether it is a contract of service or of apprenticeship or a contract personally to execute any work or labour, and includes any person ordinarily employed under any such contract, whether or not that person has been in any particular employment for any particular time.
Part II Trade disputes Article 3 Immunity of trade unions from actions in tort
(1) No action against a registered trade union, or against any member or officer of a trade union on behalf of himself and all other members thereof, in respect of any tortious act alleged to have been committed by or on behalf of the trade union in contemplation or furtherance of a trade dispute shall be entertained by any court.
(2) Nothing in this section shall affect the liability of a registered trade union or its officers in any action in respect of any property or right vested in the union, except in respect of a tortious act committed by or on behalf of the union in contemplation or furtherance of a trade dispute.
Article 4 Joint offences in relation to trade disputes
(1) An agreement or combination of two or more persons to do or procure to be done any act in contemplation or furtherance of a trade dispute shall not be punishable as a conspiracy if the act, when committed by one person, is not a criminal offence.
(2) An act done in pursuance of an agreement or combination of two or more persons, if done in contemplation or furtherance of a trade dispute, shall not be actionable unless the act, if done without that agreement or combination, would be actionable.
(3) Nothing in this section shall affect the law relating to riot, unlawful assembly, breach of the peace or sedition, or any offence against the Government or His Majesty the Sultan, the Head of State.
(4) An offence referred to in this section means an offence committed by the person accused which is punishable with imprisonment absolutely or by any other method at the discretion of the court.
(5) A person convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for an act done, or procured to be done, in pursuance of such agreement or combination shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 3 years, or, where the act is done by one person and the law otherwise provides, to imprisonment for a term exceeding 3 years.
Article 5 Protection from liability for interference with another's business An act done by a person in contemplation or furtherance of a trade dispute shall not be actionable unless it induces another person to break a contract of employment or interferes with the trade, business or employment of another person, or with the right of another person to dispose of his capital or his labour as he wills.
Article 6 Intimidation and nuisance
(1) A person who, with a view to compelling another person to abstain from doing or to do any act which that other person has a legal right to do or abstain from doing, wrongfully and without legal authority— (a) uses violence to or intimidates that other person, or his wife or children, or injures his property;
(b) persistently follows that other person from place to place;
(c) hides any tools, clothes or other property owned or used by that other person, or deprives him of or hinders him in the use thereof;
(d) watches or besets the house or other place where that other person resides, works or carries on business, or happens to be, or the approach to that house or place; or (e) follows that other person in a disorderly manner in or through any street or road, is guilty of an offence and shall be liable to imprisonment for 3 months or a fine of 3,000 Brunei dollars.
(2) Attendance at or approach to any house or place in such numbers or in such manner as is declared by section 14(2) to be unlawful shall be deemed to be a watching or besetting of that house or place within subsection (1).
Article 7 Breach of contract in respect of essential services
(1) A person who provides an essential service and who wilfully breaches or terminates his contract of service, thereby depriving the public, wholly or to a great extent, of the enjoyment of that service, knowing or having reasonable cause to believe that the probable consequence of his so doing, whether done by him alone or in combination with others, will be that result, is guilty of an offence and shall be liable to imprisonment for 3 months and a fine of 6,000 Brunei dollars.
Provided that where a collective withdrawal of labour from an essential service is planned, whether or not with a view to provoking a trade dispute, and written notice of the plan to take part in that withdrawal is given, whether by the persons providing the service or by a registered trade union representing those persons or of which those persons are members, those persons shall not be liable under this subsection unless they breach or terminate their contracts of service within 28 days after the notice is served.
(2) His Majesty the Prime Minister may make regulations prescribing the form and manner of the notice referred to in the preceding subsection.
(3) A person who incites, instigates or in any way encourages, persuades or influences a person providing an essential service to breach or terminate his contract of service, thereby depriving the public, wholly or to a great extent, of the enjoyment of that service, knowing or having reasonable cause to believe that the probable consequence of his so doing, whether done by him alone or in combination with others, will be that result, is guilty of an offence and shall be liable to imprisonment for 3 months and a fine of 6,000 Brunei dollars.
(4) An employer of an essential service shall post a copy of this section in a conspicuous place, readily readable by employees, at all premises used for the provision of that service, and shall reasonably replace it if the copy is defaced, obliterated, damaged or torn down.
(5) An employer other than the Government who fails to comply with the preceding subsection is guilty of an offence and shall be liable to a fine of 500 Brunei dollars for each day during which the non-compliance continues.
(6) A person who unlawfully damages, defaces, obliterates, destroys or tears down a copy of this Act posted under subsection (3) is guilty of an offence and shall be liable to a fine of 3,000 Brunei dollars.
(7) For the purposes of this section— (a) the following public services are essential services, namely electricity, fire, gas, health, hospital, sanitation, water supply and such other services as His Majesty the Prime Minister may declare to be subject to this Act;
(b) save as otherwise provided in this Act.
The expression “employer” includes the Government, and the expressions “person employed” and “persons employed” include persons employed by the Government.
Article 8 Breach of contract endangering life or property
(1) A person who wilfully breaches or terminates a contract of service or of employment, whether acting alone or in concert, in circumstances which endanger the life of another person or cause serious bodily injury to another person, or cause destruction of or serious damage to valuable property of another person, whether movable or immovable, knowing or having reasonable cause to believe that the probable consequence of his so doing will be that result, is guilty of an offence and shall be liable to imprisonment for 3 months and a fine of 3,000 Brunei dollars.
(2) A person who incites, instigates or in any way encourages, persuades or influences another person to breach or terminate a contract of service or of employment, in circumstances which endanger the life of another person or cause serious bodily injury to another person, or cause destruction of or serious damage to valuable property of another person, whether movable or immovable, knowing or having reasonable cause to believe that the probable consequence of that other person's so doing will be that result, is guilty of an offence and shall be liable to imprisonment for 3 months and a fine of 3,000 Brunei dollars.
Article 9 Illegal strikes and lock-outs A strike or lock-out shall be illegal if it is commenced, declared or continued in contravention of section 7 or section 8 or of any other written law:
Provided that a lock-out declared in consequence of an illegal strike, or a strike declared in consequence of an illegal lock-out, shall not be deemed to be illegal.
Article 10 Penalty for illegal strikes and lock-outs
(1) A workman who commences, continues or otherwise acts in furtherance of a strike which is illegal under this Act is guilty of an offence and shall be liable to a fine of 600 Brunei dollars and imprisonment for 1 month.
(2) An employer who commences, continues or otherwise acts in furtherance of a lock-out which is illegal under this Act is guilty of an offence and shall be liable to a fine of 6,000 Brunei dollars and imprisonment for 1 month.
Article 11 Penalty for financing illegal strikes and lock-outs A person who wilfully and directly furthers or supports an illegal strike or lock-out by expending or contributing money is guilty of an offence and shall be liable to a fine of 6,000 Brunei dollars and imprisonment for 1 month.
Article 12 Prosecution
(1) No prosecution shall be instituted for an offence under section 7, 8, 10 or 11 without the written consent of the Attorney General.
(2) Where the Government is the employer and has failed to perform the obligations of an employer under section 7(3), no person shall be prosecuted for an offence under section 7, 8, 10 or 11.
Article 13 Protection of persons refusing to take part in illegal strikes or lock-outs
(1) Notwithstanding anything in the rules of a trade union or association, a person who refuses to take part in or to continue to take part in a strike or lock-out which is illegal under this Act or any other written law shall not, by reason of that refusal or of any action taken by him under this section, be expelled from the trade union or association, or be subjected to any fine or penalty, or be deprived, or have his legal personal representative deprived, of any right or benefit, or be placed under any disability or disadvantage, directly or indirectly, in any respect as compared with other members of the trade union or association.
(2) No written law shall restrict any action entertained by a court, and no provision in the rules of a trade union or association relating to the manner of settling disputes shall apply to an action for the enforcement of a right or immunity conferred by this section, and in such an action the court may order payment from the funds of the trade union or association of such compensation or damages as the court considers reasonable, in lieu of ordering the restoration of the membership of a person who has been expelled.
Article 14 Peaceful picketing and prevention of intimidation
(1) Notwithstanding anything in this Act, it shall be lawful for one or more persons, acting on their own behalf or on behalf of a registered trade union, an employer or a company, in contemplation or furtherance of a trade dispute, to attend at or near a house or place where a person resides or works or carries on business or happens to be, if they so attend merely for the purpose of peacefully obtaining or communicating information or of peacefully persuading any person to work or to abstain from working.
(2) It shall be unlawful for one or more persons, acting on their own behalf or on behalf of a registered trade union, an employer or a company, in contemplation or furtherance of a trade dispute, to attend at or near a house or place where a person resides or works or carries on business or happens to be, if they so attend in such numbers or otherwise in such manner as to be calculated to intimidate any person in that house or place, or to obstruct the approach thereto or egress therefrom, or to lead to a breach of the peace.
(3) A person who contravenes this section is guilty of an offence and shall be liable to imprisonment for 3 months and a fine of 3,000 Brunei dollars.
Part III Arbitration and inquiry Article 15 Application
(1) This Part shall not apply to any member of the armed forces, the police force or the prisons department.
(2) Subject to subsection (1), this Part applies to workmen employed by or under the control of the Government in the same manner as to persons employed and managed privately.
Article 16 Settlement of disputes by existing machinery Where in any trade or industry there is an arrangement for the settlement of disputes in that trade or industry or any branch thereof by conciliation or arbitration, under an agreement between organisations of employers and organisations of workmen respectively representing a substantial proportion of the employers and workmen engaged in that trade or industry— (a) the Minister shall not refer the matter for settlement under section 19 unless and until the dispute cannot be or has not been settled by that arrangement; and (b) the Commissioner of Labour shall not exercise his powers under section 17(1)(c) unless and until the dispute cannot be or has not been settled by that arrangement.
Article 17 Conciliation and inquiry
(1) Where a trade dispute exists or is apprehended by the Commissioner of Labour, he shall, for the purpose of promoting the settlement of the dispute by conciliation— (a) inquire into the causes and circumstances of the dispute;
(b) take such steps as he considers appropriate to bring the parties to the dispute together, in person or by their representatives, with a view to an amicable settlement; and (c) under section 16, appoint a person as conciliator, who shall, where possible, be appointed with the agreement of both the employers and workmen concerned.
(2) A conciliator appointed under subsection (1) shall have power to inquire into the causes and circumstances of the trade dispute and to consult the parties with a view to settling the dispute, and shall report his progress to the Commissioner of Labour and, where a settlement is reached, submit to the Commissioner a memorandum of the terms signed by the representatives of both parties.
(3) The Commissioner of Labour shall, in exercising his powers under this section, report to the Minister.
Article 18 Report of dispute to the Minister for consideration and settlement Any trade dispute existing or apprehended may be reported to the Minister by or on behalf of either party to the dispute, and the Minister shall forthwith consider it and take such steps as he considers appropriate to settle it.
Article 19 Arbitration: reference of dispute to arbitration tribunal and constitution of tribunal
(1) Under section 16 and with the agreement of both parties, the Minister may refer an existing or apprehended trade dispute to an arbitration tribunal.
(2) A tribunal shall be constituted as follows— (a) a sole arbitrator appointed by His Majesty the Sultan;
(b) one arbitrator appointed by His Majesty, assisted by one or more experts appointed by the employers concerned or their representatives and an equal number of experts appointed by the workmen concerned or their representatives, all of whom shall be appointed by His Majesty the Sultan; but the award shall be made and published by the arbitrator alone; or (c) one or more arbitrators appointed by the employers concerned or their representatives and an equal number of arbitrators appointed by the workmen concerned or their representatives, together with an independent chairman, all of whom shall be appointed by His Majesty the Sultan:
Provided that where all the members of the tribunal fail to agree on an award, the matter shall be determined by the chairman as sole arbitrator.
Article 20 Vacancies in tribunal
(1) Where a tribunal consists of one arbitrator assisted by several experts, and a vacancy occurs in the number of experts, the tribunal may act at the discretion of the arbitrator or agree to appoint another expert to fill the vacancy.
Any such new expert shall be appointed by the party that originally appointed the expert whose place is vacant.
(2) No act, proceeding or award of a tribunal shall be questioned or invalidated by reason of any such vacancy.
Article 21 Publication of award
(1) Every award of a tribunal shall be submitted to the Minister, who shall publish it as soon as possible in such manner as he considers appropriate.
(2) Where the public or the news media are not permitted to attend the sittings of a tribunal, no award, report or other publication made or authorised by the tribunal or the Minister, and no information obtained from the tribunal in the course of the arbitration relating to a trade union or an independent undertaking, whether carried on by an individual, a partnership or a company, and which could not otherwise be obtained except as evidence at those sittings, shall be published except with the consent of the secretary general of the trade union or of the individual, partnership or company carrying on the undertaking, as the case may be.
(3) Where the public or the news media are not permitted to attend the sittings of a tribunal, no member of the tribunal, person connected with the sittings or person attending the sittings of the tribunal shall disclose any information obtained from the tribunal in the course of the arbitration relating to a trade union or an independent undertaking, whether carried on by an individual, a partnership or a company, and which could not otherwise be obtained except as evidence at those sittings, except with the consent of the secretary general of the trade union or of the individual, partnership or company carrying on the undertaking, as the case may be.
(4) A person who contravenes this section is guilty of an offence and shall be liable to a fine of 3,000 Brunei dollars.
Article 22 Interpretation of award Any question arising as to the interpretation of an award made by a tribunal may be referred by the Minister or by any party to the award to the tribunal for decision, and the tribunal shall decide the question after hearing the parties or, without such hearing, with the consent of the parties. The tribunal shall notify its decision to the parties, and the decision shall be deemed to form part of the original award and shall have the same effect in all respects as the original award.
Article 23 Evidence For the purpose of settling a trade dispute referred under section 19, a tribunal shall have full power to order, in the same manner as the High Court makes orders, any person to furnish information in writing or in such other manner as the tribunal may require on matters relevant to the dispute, and where necessary to attend before the tribunal and give evidence on oath and to produce documents, so as to obtain all information relevant to the matters in dispute, and where necessary shall not be bound by the rules of evidence in civil or criminal proceedings:
Provided that a witness who refuses to answer a question on the ground that the answer may incriminate him, or on other lawful grounds, shall not be required to answer it and shall not be liable to any penalty for refusing to answer.
Article 24 Appearance by counsel A tribunal may, at its discretion on the request of counsel, permit any interested person to appear and participate in arbitration proceedings under this Act.
Article 25 Sittings public or private The tribunal may at its discretion decide whether to permit the public or the news media to attend the arbitration sittings.
Article 26 Publication of arbitration proceedings Whether or not the news media are permitted to attend the arbitration sittings, a full and accurate report or summary of the arbitration, including the evidence produced at the sittings, shall be published:
Provided that no comment on the arbitration proceedings or the evidence shall be published before the award is published by order of the Minister.
A person who contravenes this section is guilty of an offence and shall be liable to imprisonment for 6 months and a fine of 6,000 Brunei dollars.
Article 27 Rules of procedure His Majesty the Prime Minister may make regulations prescribing the procedure to be followed by a tribunal, and in respect of any matter arising in the course of arbitration for which no rule has been provided, the tribunal may regulate its own procedure.
Article 28 Costs of arbitration The Minister may, in accordance with the directions of His Majesty the Prime Minister, pay to arbitrators or experts appointed under this Act remuneration exceeding their ordinary income.
Article 29 Posting of copies of the Act as directed by the Commissioner of Labour Copies of this Act shall be posted at such places and in such languages as the Commissioner of Labour may direct.
Article 30 Special provisions Nothing in this Act authorises a member of the armed forces or a police officer or an officer of the prisons department to take part in a lock-out or strike in contravention of this Act.
